title: FORTY MINUTES ON THE SAME ROPE
deck: A cable car stalls a hundred and ninety metres short of the summit that could end an eleven-year war, and the two envoys aboard carry sealed orders that forbid each other's clause. Illuminara cannot carry them, cannot sign for them and will not decide for them; she has a stopped car, failing air, a hand-winch that needs everyone's breath, and one question she has to get exactly right.
shape: Six scenes run from the stall to the summit hall. The first sets a hand-winch, a rhythm, Illuminara's refusal to carry anyone and a student's stray rule about the Chair's record; the second finds the same word in both sets of orders; the third and fourth give each envoy a long rest in which to say one true thing, let the two crewmen who live where the bill would land say what would make it bearable, and turn Illuminara's quiet help with the air into a choice the others make; the fifth wrecks two drafts, then builds a clause whose first sentences must be spoken in the hall before the vote; and the last puts the clause in front of a delegate with sealed orders and a Reach delegate who wrote the form, then the first quiet night of the war and a year-on anniversary in the rain.

scenes.title: Car Seven
paragraphs: *Sky Hook car 7, a hundred and ninety metres short of Meridian Station · 14:09, fifty-one minutes before the ceasefire ends*

The car stopped the way a held breath stops. There was no jolt, only everything that had been moving remembering it could not. The cabin lights went amber. The hum in the floor, which Illuminara had stopped hearing somewhere above the clouds, became the loudest thing in the world by being gone.

Six people. Ambassador Tamsin Okoro-Vael of the Reach sat very straight with a locked dispatch case across her knees and a silver braid pinned up like a decision. Envoy Dathe Quillon of the Compact stood by the far door with his own case chained to his wrist; he was young, and he had been standing since Sable Landing. A cable engineer in a yellow vest, Hollis Vane, was already on his back under a panel. Beside the left crank sat a hauler off the Sable Landing shift, Pell Amadi, with a lunch tin between his boots, saying nothing at all. A student with a registry lanyard, Noor Haddad, held a box of treaty binders against her chest as if it might float away.

**Hollis** 
That's the Shade. Thirty-eight kilometres of tether where the field eats every signal, and we ran all of it and stopped a hundred and ninety metres short of the Meridian cradle, which is the first place anyone could hear us. Brake's set. The scrubbers went with the main bus. Truce rule, every Sky Hook shift is half and half: I'm the Reach hand today, Pell's the Compact one. On paper that's a full crew.

**Dathe** 
How long is the air?

**Hollis** 
Half an hour that you'd call good. After that you'd feel it.

**Tamsin** 
The ceasefire expires at fifteen hundred. If there are no delegations seated at Meridian by then, both fleets sail.

**Hollis** 
Then it's the crank. Two stations, one capstan, forty centimetres a stroke. Twelve strokes a minute and the cradle is forty minutes up the line. Miss two beats together and the ratchet slips.

Illuminara had said nothing yet. She stood in the middle of the cabin with her light dimmed to a lamp's worth, and she could feel the whole frame of the car, every rivet, as one held thing. She could have lifted it. She had known that the moment it stopped.

**Illuminara** 
I can carry this car to Meridian in ninety seconds. Or any one of you, or all of you. If any of you asks me, I will, and nobody here will think less of you for it. I want that said first.
Nobody asked. The amber light ticked on the tether's frost.

**Tamsin** 
If you carry me in, my minister's first question is who carried me.

**Dathe** 
Mine is what was said on the way.

**Illuminara** 
Yes. I would rather not be the answer to either question. I will keep the frame whole and the air breathable. I will not move the car and I will not sign anything. The rope is yours.

Hollis rolled out from under the panel and looked at the six of them as if counting a crew. Noor, who had said nothing since the stall, started to speak the way some people hum, to keep from hearing the silence.

**Noor** 
Standing Order Fourteen. Anything said from the floor before the Chair puts the question goes into the Chair's record, and the Chair can't strike it. I copy it every session. It's the only rule I know by heart.

**Illuminara** 
For both delegations?

**Noor** 
Both. The Compact wrote it, in the first year, so the Reach couldn't tidy their speeches afterwards. The Reach wrote the half about the Chair not being able to strike it, so the Compact couldn't either.
It was a stranger's fact, offered to a stalled car, and Illuminara put it away the way one pockets a key one does not yet have a door for.

**Hollis** 
Haul on one-two. Breathe on three-four. Every tenth minute the capstan needs thirty seconds to cool, and that's the only time anybody speaks longer than two counts.

scenes.title: The Same Word
paragraphs: *Car 7, the first ten minutes · 14:12*

They sorted themselves without discussion. Hollis and Pell took the left crank. Tamsin took the right and, after one look at the envoy across from her, so did Dathe. Noor held the brake lever and the count. Illuminara stood in the middle of the cabin and let the car's weight pass through her like a note through a bell, and breathed for the room.
One-two. The handles came round with a groan. Three-four. Six people took the same breath, because the rhythm would not allow another.
By the fourth minute the car had risen nineteen metres and Illuminara had learned that nobody speaks in two-count sentences who wants to lie. It was the first mercy of the rope.

**Illuminara** 
I am not going to ask what is in your envelopes.

**Dathe** 
Good.

**Illuminara** 
I am going to ask what you were told they say.
The cabin creaked up through the dark.

**Tamsin** 
Refuse Clause Nine. Unless it contains the word recognise.
One-two. Three-four.

**Dathe** 
Refuse Clause Nine. If it contains the word recognise.
Noor made a noise that was half a laugh and half a hiccup, and apologised for it.

**Hollis** 
Same word.

**Dathe** 
It is not funny, Mr Vane.

**Tamsin** 
It is the only joke eleven years of war has produced. Let him have it.
They kept hauling. At the ninth minute the strongest thing either of them had said so far came from the envoy of the Compact, who had stopped looking at his hands.

**Dathe** 
Understand me. These are not stupid orders. Someone in the capital was afraid that the Reach would make us sign a confession and call it peace. I am afraid of that too. If I hear what the Ambassador means by the word, and it is reasonable, I must disobey, and my government will say I was bought in a lift.

**Tamsin** 
And if the Compact will not say the word, it does not say it happened. That is not stubbornness either, Envoy.

Illuminara set the two orders side by side in her mind as if they were two halves of a torn page, and they fitted. One side wanted a sentence heard; the other feared a sentence filed. They were asking for the same object from opposite ends of its life, and neither knew the other's end was the one that frightened them. That was a diagnosis, not a solution. A diagnosis would not lift a car. She did not say it.
The capstan began to smoke a little, the way rope does when it has been asked for too much honest work. Hollis called the long rest.

**Illuminara** 
Then I will ask only this, and you may answer in your own time. Tell me what each of you is afraid the other will do with the word.

scenes.title: Casualty of Operations
paragraphs: *Car 7, the first long rest · 14:22*
Thirty seconds. Six people breathing, the cabin cold enough now to show it. Tamsin kept both hands on the crank as if letting go would cost her the car.

**Tamsin** 
Pael was my brother. He ran the ferry at the Narrows, the small one, the one with the blue hull. Second year of the war. A shell came across the strait in the morning. The paper that reached my mother said casualty of operations. No name on the line. A number.
She did not look at Dathe. She said it flat, as one gives an address to a clerk for the fortieth time.

**Tamsin** 
I do not want money. I have been accused of wanting money for eleven years, by people who would not have it said that anyone died on that boat. I want one person on your side to say out loud that a person died. Not a number. A word is the only way my brother becomes a man in your mouth.
One-two. The handles came round. Dathe had not moved. Hollis, on the left crank, had gone very still at the words blue hull.

**Dathe** 
What did he teach?

**Tamsin** 
What?

**Dathe** 
You said ferry. A man with a small ferry usually has a trade beside it.

**Tamsin** 
He taught children to swim. In the shallows, in the summer, off the stern.

**Hollis** 
He let us steer her. Off the end of the pier, when the tide was slack. I was nine.
Dathe's hands came off the crank.

The ratchet slipped. The car dropped a hand's breadth with a shriek of pawls, and the cabin tilted, and Noor said a short word. Illuminara closed her will around the frame before the dogs could bite crooked. She held the car where it was, not lifting it, only refusing the tilt, and felt the weight of six lives settle in her like a bag of water.

Across from him, the Ambassador took Dathe's handle in her left hand and her own in her right. She hauled two cranks' worth for four counts. She did not speak. She did not look at him. When his hands found the grip again she let it go.

**Dathe** 
I did not mean to stop.

**Tamsin** 
I know.

Illuminara let out a breath she did not need. In the middle of the rope, between the cold and the creak, she felt something small and clean and entirely her own: she was not needed for this. Five pairs of hands were doing what her strength could not do for them, and the pleasure of it startled her.

scenes.title: What Would Make It Bearable
paragraphs: *Car 7, the second long rest · 14:32*
Near the top of the Shade the air began to taste of rust. Hollis tapped the gauge on the panel twice, looked at it, and then looked at Illuminara for longer than a gauge deserved.

**Hollis** 
By my bottle we should be feeling it by now. We aren't. Something's holding the air past what I told you.

**Illuminara** 
I am. A little at a time, since the last rest. I did not ask you, and I should have. I will stop if you say stop.

**Hollis** 
Don't stop.

**Tamsin** 
Do it where we can see you doing it.

**Dathe** 
And tell us when it is more than you can hold.

**Illuminara** 
Yes. All three.
It was a small thing and it cost her nothing but the asking, and it changed how the cold felt. Then she turned to the envoy.

**Illuminara** 
Envoy. Your turn, if you want it.

**Dathe** 
Ilmar Strand. My mother's village. Thirty years ago. The Compact turned on its own. A purge. You will know it. She walked out with a bag. The neighbours who hid people, they were not the ones who gave the orders. They were the ones who stayed.
One-two. Three-four.

**Dathe** 
When the war began the Reach said the Compact had done these things. It was true. And the bill, every time, went to whoever was nearest and still speaking Compact. A woman called Hesh. Spat on, in a market. Three hundred kilometres from anything she had done.

**Tamsin** 
Three hundred and ten. I have the file.

**Dathe** 
You have a file.
Tamsin's hands tightened on the crank, and for a count she said nothing.

**Tamsin** 
I should not have said the number.

**Dathe** 
Blame does not fall on the guilty, Ambassador. It falls on whoever is nearest. In a court in the Reach, the word recognise is a notice sent to villages like my mother's.

**Tamsin** 
I do not send bills to villages.

**Dathe** 
You do not choose where it goes once it is written.

Illuminara listened to the rope. Under the two voices there was a pattern, and she turned toward it carefully, the way one turns an ear toward a sound one has stopped trusting. Every fear in the car, she noticed, had the same grammar: a thing written travels. A signature leaves the room, goes to a ministry, becomes a notice. A sentence stays where it was said. But that was an inference from two speeches, and the man most likely to know whether it was true was sitting on the left crank with a lunch tin between his boots.

**Illuminara** 
Pell. Two counts, then the rest, if you will. Is Ilmar Strand yours?

**Pell** 
My mother. Harbour Row.
One-two. Three-four. Pell's face did what faces do when a person has been invisible on purpose for thirty minutes.

**Pell** 
I never said, Envoy. Didn't think it was mine to say.

**Illuminara** 
I am not going to ask you to speak for her. I am asking so I know whether I am hearing something or imagining it. If a woman of the Reach stood in your mother's street and said one hard true thing aloud, what would have to be so, for it not to be a notice?

**Pell** 
That she asked first. That the street could say no. That she didn't read it off a page.

**Illuminara** 
Mr Vane. The Narrows?

**Hollis** 
Near enough the same, and no flags. Pael's boat is not a stage. If a man of the Compact came, the families would want to pick the hour, and they'd want it said on the pier quiet, the way you tell somebody at a door. Maybe they'd not want it at all. They'd want to be able to not want it.

**Illuminara** 
Then I notice that neither of you named a document. You named who asks, who may refuse, and who listens.
Nobody answered on the next two counts, because the rope would not allow it. When the long rest came, it was Tamsin who spoke, and she did not lift her eyes from the crank.

**Tamsin** 
Unsigned means deniable. A man says it in a village and my minister says wind, and I have gone home with a promise.

**Illuminara** 
Then tell me what would make it impossible for your minister to say wind.

**Tamsin** 
That it is not I who says it happened. That someone of the Compact says it, in a place where a Compact person heard, and the hearer can say so afterwards in my capital, and nobody can send her home.

**Dathe** 
And mine cannot call it bought if it was said where the village could hear it and its own hands kept the record.
They had each described the same object. Neither of them had noticed.

**Noor** 
There's a form for it. In the registry. A place consents to a visit. Nobody has used it for anything but funerals.

**Hollis** 
Then use it for one.
Hollis called the last stretch. The cabin lights flickered and held.

scenes.title: Two Drafts and a Card
paragraphs: *Car 7, the final stretch · 14:41*
They wrote it in the long rests, a line at a time, on the back of Noor's registry card with a pencil from Hollis's vest. The first draft was a speech. Dathe read it aloud and heard himself reading.

**Dathe** 
This is a confession in costume. Give me this paper in the village and it is a notice.
The second draft was a loophole. The Compact acknowledges that losses occurred in the course of operations. Tamsin read it once and put her finger on the sentence.

**Tamsin** 
That is the grammar of my mother's paper. Losses occurred. No one did anything to anyone. You would have me trade a casualty for a casualty.

She tore that card in half herself and handed him the halves. Noor produced another, and tape. Nobody spoke for six counts. Then Illuminara, who had promised not to write and had not, spoke into the rope.

**Illuminara** 
I will not draft it. I will say what I notice. You have each told me you will be disowned. Disowned is what happens to a person who says a thing after a vote, in the hands of whoever counts the votes. But Noor gave us a rule an hour ago and none of us has used it. What is said from the floor before the question is put goes into the Chair's record, and the Chair cannot strike it. Nobody can disown a sentence that a whole hall has heard and the Chair has already written down. If your first sentences are spoken before the vote, they are no longer a promise to be argued about. They are a fact the hall has to vote around.

**Illuminara** 
Noor. Does the Chair have any discretion over that?

**Noor** 
Over the order of business. Not over the record. I've watched them try.

**Tamsin** 
He would be recalled by morning.

**Dathe** 
So would you.

**Tamsin** 
I may be.
What stood on the card at 14:47 was six sentences in pencil, in the cramped hand of a person who copied for a living.

*For the first anniversary of this treaty, Ambassador Okoro-Vael and Envoy Quillon shall each go to the other party's place of mourning, the Narrows and Ilmar Strand, on a day and in a manner the hosts there set. The hosts may decline; a declined day is waited out in their presence, not forced. The visitor says there whatever the visitor finds to say, the hosts keep the only record, and what is said is said by that person alone. No claim, levy or reprisal shall be founded on it against any party or any place. If a visitor does not come, the host writes the absence in the book and the other visitor goes anyway. Before this is voted, each of the two who wrote it shall say one sentence of their own, in the hall.*

**Tamsin** 
It does not contain the word.

**Dathe** 
No.

**Tamsin** 
I wanted a clause that obliges them. This obliges two people to go and stand somewhere.

**Dathe** 
Yes.

**Tamsin** 
A minister can call words wind. He cannot call a village's book wind. It is not his.

Neither of them had signed it, because there was nothing to sign. They looked at each other across the capstan for the first time since Sable Landing, two people in damp wool who could see how the next week would go: the ministers' faces, the editorials, the word taken in a lift.

**Tamsin** 
They will say you were bought.

**Dathe** 
They will say you were taken in.

**Tamsin** 
Then we will say the same thing in the same hall.

**Pell** 
It's forty minutes of rope, Envoy. I counted them. We're nearly out.
At 14:51 the cabin shuddered, found the cradle, and the doors opened on light.

scenes.title: The Hall
paragraphs: *Meridian Station, the summit hall · 14:58, two minutes before the ceasefire would have ended*

The Chair of the summit, Imelda Sorn, had held the doors for the length of one cigarette. A technician had put car seven's stall on her monitor at 14:09, and she had been smoking slowly ever since. Two fleets lay at anchor on opposite sides of the strait with their engines warm. Pell, Hollis and Noor stayed at the back with Illuminara. The envoys walked the aisle with a pencilled card between them, and the hall went quiet the way water goes quiet before a boat.
Sorn stood at the dais when the Compact's first delegate rose. Delegate Orsin Kerr had sealed orders, and he held them up in front of him like a warrant.

**Kerr** 
My orders forbid Clause Nine in any form. Two envoys went up a cable in a closed car, nobody heard them for fifty minutes, and they have come down with a text no government has seen. Why should this hall believe a car?

**Sorn** 
Who rode with them, who is not theirs?
Three hands went up at the back, none of them hers. The hall turned, and Illuminara felt every eye reach her, pass on, and settle on the three who had raised theirs. She was glad to be passed over.

**Kerr** 
You. The one with the lunch tin. You are Compact. Do you want this said at Ilmar Strand?

**Pell** 
I wasn't asked. I'm asked now.
He stood with his hands flat on his thighs the way he had stood at the crank.

**Pell** 
I want my mother asked. If she says not like this, then not like this. If she says come, then the Ambassador knocks on Harbour Row like a neighbour and nobody in this hall reads a word to her.

**Sorn** 
And the Narrows?

**Hollis** 
Not with flags. The families choose the hour. Put that in or leave the ferry alone.
Sorn read the card, then the pencilled line about the hosts, then looked at the envoys over her glasses.

**Sorn** 
The hosts set the day and the manner and may refuse. That is in the text. I will have it voted as written.

**Kerr** 
Nothing is written. A sentence in a village is wind.

**Dathe** 
Then let it be wind, Delegate. Here it is.
He did not have a paper. His hand on the chain at his wrist was not steady, and he took the hand off the chain.

**Dathe** 
A man called Pael Okoro-Vael ran the small ferry at the Narrows, the one with the blue hull. In the second year a shell from the Compact's side killed him on a morning crossing. I say this as myself. My government has not said it.
Nobody in the hall made a sound. Tamsin stood.

**Tamsin** 
Thirty years ago a purge drove the mother of Envoy Quillon out of Ilmar Strand with a bag. The neighbours who hid people were not the ones who gave the orders. The Reach has billed their village for it for eleven years. I say this as myself. My government has not said it.

**Kerr** 
You have both ended your careers.

**Tamsin** 
Probably.
Sorn did not look up from the card. She spoke to the record, in the voice of a woman reading a timetable.

**Sorn** 
Standing Order Fourteen. Both sentences were said from the floor before the question was put. They are in the Chair's record. I cannot strike them, Delegate, and neither can you.
Kerr stood a long time with the sealed orders in his hand. His orders had forbidden a clause. They had not foreseen two sentences already said.

Across the aisle a woman of the Reach rose, grey-haired, with the heavy walk of someone who had spent thirty years in an office. Delegate Maren Tolle did not go to the dais. She said it from where she stood.

**Tolle** 
Chair, a sentence in a village is wind. A sentence in a village is —
She stopped. She was looking at Tamsin, not at the Chair.

**Tolle** 
The second year. Casualty of operations. No name on the line.

**Tamsin** 
That is the paper my mother received.

**Tolle** 
I ran that office. I wrote the form. It had a box for a number and none for a name, because a name makes a clerk hesitate.
She did not sit. The Reach delegates behind her turned their heads, one by one, the way a field turns.

**Tolle** 
I did not know there was a boat. I will second the clause. Not because it is kind. Because I have never in my life been asked to say a name, and I would like to be.

**Kerr** 
Mine say refuse. I will vote against, and I will say why, and it will not be because I think a car is a liar.

The summit began at 15:00 and ten seconds. The hall was loud for three hours. The Reach delegation split behind Tolle; the Compact's elders voted against it in committee, and the envoy's name was struck from the delegation list for a week, so that he read about it on the way to bed. At 18:20 the plenary adopted Clause Nine by seven votes to four. The fleets did not sail.
That night the strait was quiet for the first time in eleven years, and the ferry at the Narrows, the small one with the blue hull, made its crossing at dusk with the lights on.

A year later it rained. The families had chosen the hour and the pier and no flags, and a woman who had learned to float in the shallows off the ferry's stern stood at the front of the small crowd in a coat that did not keep the wet out. Envoy Dathe Quillon stood where the first name was cut, with no paper, and did not say anything for a long time.

Illuminara stood at the back, beside a student with a registry lanyard, who had come to copy and had stayed to listen. Across the strait, on Harbour Row, a door had opened for the Ambassador of the Reach in worse weather. A woman with a lunch tin on her table had asked her to come in out of it.

**Noor** 
What is he finding to say?

**Illuminara** 
I don't know. Nobody does. Not even him, yet.
Then he spoke, in his own words, and the rain took the first sentence and the woman in the front row heard it anyway.

critic_line: Illuminara refuses to carry or command and instead notices that two mirrored fears ask for the same thing from opposite ends of its life, so that two grieving envoys, the people who live where the blame would land, and a Chair's own standing rule let a clause be spoken in the hall before the vote and the fleets do not sail.
